summary: A Network Host Status report covering July 3 to July 14, 1972. Testing was skipped on July 4 for the holiday and on July 11 and 12 because the author was away. It was replaced by RFC 370.

plainLanguage.summary: This report records which ARPANET hosts could be reached during a period in July 1972. Its status marks distinguish successful connections from hosts that were unavailable, busy, or did not respond as expected.

questions: which arpanet hosts could be reached
what do the host status marks mean
subtitle: A July 1972 report of which ARPANET hosts answered connection tests.

tldr.problem: Network users needed a record of which hosts could be reached during the reporting period.
tldr.mechanism: The report records connection-test results from July 3 to July 14, excluding days when testing was not done, and defines the status marks used in its tables.
tldr.outcome: It provides a dated snapshot of host reachability. RFC 370 replaced it.

today: RFC 367 was replaced by RFC 370. It records host status for a period in July 1972.

sections.title: The Reporting Period
sections.content: RFC 367 reports on the status of most network hosts from July 3 to July 14, 1972. Testing did not take place on July 4 or July 11 and 12. The report explains that those gaps were due to a holiday and the author's vacation.
sections.plainLanguage: The report gives a snapshot of host availability over a period in July 1972. It has no test results for three days when testing was not done.

sections.title: How to Read the Status Marks
sections.content:
The tables record the result of attempts to connect to hosts. Open means a host opened a connection and was accessible; Dead means it was unreachable from the testing point. Other marks distinguish a full host, a connection that opened only partly, a refusal, or a timeout before the Initial Connection Procedure finished.

The RFC says a timeout means the connection did not complete within 60 seconds. Some hosts were not tested because they were intended only as users, rather than service providers.
sections.plainLanguage: The table uses letters to show what happened when a host was contacted. For example, “Open” means the host accepted a connection, while “Dead” means it could not be reached from the test point.

sections.title: Status of This Report
sections.content: RFC 367 is a time-specific operational report, not a protocol specification. The unit metadata records RFC 370 as its replacement.
sections.plainLanguage: This document describes network conditions during its reporting period. RFC 370 later replaced it.
